newsitem.title: FINLAND: Hopes high as Nokia probes records pre-Q2.
newsitem.headline: Hopes high as Nokia probes records pre-Q2.

text.p: International investors may need a spot of consolidation in mobile phone major Nokia's stock before they applaud a widely expected sharp increase in H1 earnings next Monday.

But markets running at record-high levels have only briefly hesitated as Nokia, once again a fast-track darling of positive surprises after a troubled patch in late 1995 and early 1996, faces potentially steep earnings expectations.
Nokia's stock has surged 70 percent this year to around 460 markka in Helsinki, settling on Monday and Tuesday but again probing all-time high ground on Wednesday following U.S. gains.

"The problem as an investor is that this sector is the fastest-growing sector in the world and you want to have a presence in it," said Lauri Rosendahl, analyst at Aros in Helsinki, earlier this week.
The company put in a bumper Q1 earnings boost, to 1.45 billion markka from 399 million in the 1996 period.
Nokia surged last week when Swedish rival Ericsson put in a surprise 44 percent boost in H1 earnings.

Only a minority of analysts polled by Reuters earlier this week said they had subsequently upgraded Nokia forecasts: the median expectation now is for a 125 percent boost in Q2 profit to about 1.64 billion markka.

However, those are official figures. Some analysts had yet to decide how high to pitch, as bulls muttered higher numbers. Of course, much hangs on how U.S. investors in broader areas respond to major data, like non-farm jobless payrolls on Friday.
Still, one analyst's "whisper number" of 50-60 percent growth in handset sales for Nokia -- against over 100 percent for smaller handset player Ericsson -- is another's minimum.
"We're looking for 57 percent, but from a weak comparative period," said another analyst, who requested anonymity but was the closest forecaster polled by Reuters for Nokia's Q1.
Many expect handset margins -- officially unstated by the company -- to have held above 10 percent. Telecommunications infrastructure sales are seen rising about 30 percent.
The gut reaction bulls are hoping for from the report is a bound in Nokia stock, delivered by a trading fraternity not looking beyond a fat increase over a very weak H1 1996.
For the half, analysts polled by Reuters expect profit to nearly triple to 3.09 billion markka from 1.13 billion in 1996. The test, if Nokia fails to surprise, will be keeping cool.
"It's not impossible to imagine the shares going down on the day even though the results are good," said Neil Barton at Merrill Lynch in London.
Sceptics focus on Nokia's relatively mature voice product range -- and the inroads Ericsson's 788 model seems to have made at the market's top end -- as a factor dulling Nokia's Q2 shine.
But, in a heavily-invested high-growth market, against that can be held the unannounced new models Nokia is expected to unveil in H2, in response to its rivals.
Asked if he felt Nokia's Q2 results would unleash major profit-taking even with spectacular results, Lehman Brothers' Jeremy Alun-Jones said: "I would attach a fairly low probability to that."

A Helsinki options source on Monday reported more bullish than defensive trades in quite thin dealings, even though Nokia's volatility had risen to the high 30s. There were also strategies to profit from volatility.
Based on that, the view may be 'prepare to take profits, a bit later'. One analyst noted that currency gains, a key element of Ericsson's strong H1, will eventually peter out.
"Phones around 100 grams will be the segment where the big players have to start to compete," said Rosendahl.
He expects Motorola, Nokia and Ericsson to try to squeeze Philips' forthcoming model, the Genie. "The second half of 1997 will show faster price declines than the first," he said.
